metadata.file_name: 62. Wang et al. (2022). Understanding Chinese Students’ Well‑Being: A Machine Learning Study.pdf
metadata.title: Understanding Chinese Students’ Well‑Being: A Machine Learning Study

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Mainland China, focusing on 15-year-old students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the random forest regression analyses, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate design (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the primary learner is random forest regression, the authors may have omitted complex-survey weighting; however, this is not explicitly justified. The analytic sample is restricted to the specified Chinese regions and further uses standardized predictors and MCMC-based multiple imputation for missing questionnaire variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are well-being dimensions measured via questionnaire Likert items (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, and meaning in life), not PV-based cognitive achievement scores. The paper therefore does not require PV generation/combination procedures typical of PISA achievement domains. Missing data handling is reported via MCMC multiple imputation, so the main transparency issue concerns survey-weight usage rather than PV handling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 Mainland China dataset publicly available from OECD, restricted to 15-year-old students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang (B-S-J-Z). Dependent variables were the four well-being dimensions operationalized from PISA 2018 questionnaire items (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, meaning in life). Predictors were selected from the PISA 2018 questionnaire constructs (background, schooling, non-cognitive/metacognitive) as listed in Table 1 (35 variables). Missing values across the investigated variables were imputed using MCMC multiple imputation before model training; predictors were standardized to zero mean and unit SD.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — R²: 21.41%, MSE: 0.79 (baseline with 35 predictors); optimal model with top 9 predictors R²: 21.41%, MSE: 0.79; importance via %IncMSE (higher = more important).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (China) 15-year-olds well-being questionnaire the study leveraged sense of school belonging, resilience, work mastery, mastery goal orientation, and parents’ emotional support to predict positive affect, finding that school belonging and resilience were the most important predictors (top-ranked and second-ranked within the selected set). This indicates that strengthening school belonging and resilience-building supports may be effective targets for interventions aimed at improving students’ positive emotions, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — R²: 19.21%, MSE: 0.81 (initial model with 35 predictors); optimal model with top 9 predictors R²: 18.13%, MSE: 0.82; importance via %IncMSE.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (China) 15-year-olds well-being questionnaire the study leveraged general fear of failure, sense of school belonging, resilience, ESCS, and reading for enjoyment to predict negative affect, finding that fear of failure and school belonging were the most important predictors (fear of failure ranked first). This indicates that reducing students’ fear of failure through supportive assessment and feedback practices, alongside improving belonging, may help lower negative emotions, while causality cannot be inferred from predictive modeling.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — R²: 26.44%, MSE: 0.74 (initial model with 35 predictors); optimal model with top 9 predictors R²: 24.14%, MSE: 0.76; importance via %IncMSE (resilience and belonging contributed large mean decreases in accuracy).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (China) 15-year-olds well-being questionnaire the study leveraged resilience, sense of school belonging, parents’ emotional support, general fear of failure, and work mastery to predict life satisfaction, finding that school belonging and resilience were the leading predictors (ranked first and second in the selected set). This indicates that family emotional support and belonging-enhancing school environments, together with resilience development, may improve students’ life satisfaction, though the study’s cross-sectional ML approach does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — R²: 32.47%, MSE: 0.68 (initial model with 35 predictors); optimal model with top 9 predictors R²: 32.47%, MSE: 0.78; importance via %IncMSE (resilience and work mastery accounted for >62% decrease in accuracy).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (China) 15-year-olds well-being questionnaire the study leveraged resilience, work mastery, sense of school belonging, parents’ emotional support, and perceived cooperation at school to predict eudaimonic well-being (meaning in life), finding that resilience and work mastery were the top predictors. This indicates that interventions promoting students’ mastery-oriented engagement and resilience may strengthen students’ sense of purpose, while the predictive nature of the evidence limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 questionnaire data for 12,058 Chinese 15-year-olds from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, predicting four well-being dimensions: positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, and meaning in life (eudaimonic well-being). The authors use random forest regression and report model fit using MSE and explained variance (R²), along with variable importance measured by %IncMSE. Across outcomes, school belonging and resilience dominate positive affect and life satisfaction, fear of failure is the top predictor for negative affect, and resilience plus work mastery are the strongest predictors for meaning in life. Missing questionnaire data are handled via MCMC multiple imputation, and predictors are standardized. The paper emphasizes predictive importance rather than causal mechanisms; additionally, it does not report the use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, which may affect generalizability under complex survey design.
